subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and neuralgia risk assessment in a dermatomal vesicular eruption
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 71 year old woman describes two days of deep burning pain across the right side of her chest that she initially thought was muscular, and since yesterday morning a rash has appeared over the same area.

There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band from the right side of the spine around to the sternum, stopping abruptly at the midline. She rates the pain at 8 out of 10 and it is stopping her sleeping. She takes ramipril and atorvastatin, has an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73m2, and is not immunosuppressed. There are no lesions on the face, no eye symptoms and no lesions crossing the midline.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles in a unilateral thoracic dermatomal band, marked allodynia over the affected skin, no ocular or facial involvement
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60); no viral swab taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe topical aciclovir cream with simple analgesia and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Topical antiviral does not penetrate adequately to affect the course of the illness or the risk of ongoing neuralgia, which requires systemic treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Withhold antiviral treatment because the rash has already been present for over 24 hours
options.rationale: The window for benefit runs to 72 hours from rash onset and extends beyond that while new vesicles are still appearing, so treatment is clearly still indicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral valaciclovir with analgesia and defer any vaccination until she has recovered
options.rationale: Oral antiviral started within 72 hours reduces the duration of the eruption and the risk of persisting neuralgia, and vaccination is given after the acute episode has resolved rather than during it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone alone for the pain and arrange review in the clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy does not reduce the risk of persisting neuralgia and is only ever considered alongside an antiviral in selected patients (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give the recombinant zoster vaccine today and prescribe oral analgesia for the acute pain
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents future episodes but has no effect on an eruption already underway, and it is deferred until the acute illness resolves (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Herpes zoster arises from reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglion and produces a painful unilateral eruption that respects the dermatome and stops at the midline. Oral antiviral therapy started within 72 hours of rash onset shortens the acute illness and reduces the incidence and severity of postherpetic neuralgia, and it should still be given beyond that window while new vesicles continue to form or when there is ophthalmic, disseminated or immunosuppressed disease. The complication that dominates morbidity is postherpetic neuralgia, whose risk rises steeply with age and with the severity of acute pain, and it is treated with amitriptyline, nortriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin rather than with simple analgesia alone. In Australia the recombinant subunit zoster vaccine has replaced the live attenuated product, is given as two doses, and is funded for older adults and for people who are immunocompromised, in whom the live vaccine was contraindicated.
key_points: Treat within 72 hours of rash onset, and later while new vesicles are still appearing
Ophthalmic, disseminated and immunosuppressed disease always warrant antiviral therapy
Severe acute pain and older age are the main predictors of postherpetic neuralgia
Corticosteroids do not reduce postherpetic neuralgia risk
The recombinant zoster vaccine is a two dose course suitable for immunocompromised people
explanation.pearls: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and predict ocular disease, so that finding warrants same day ophthalmology review even when the eye itself looks normal.

subtopic_detail: Serological workup of an occupationally acquired zoonosis and pre vaccination screening requirements
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a regional Queensland hospital. A 32 year old man who has worked in an abattoir for six weeks presents with ten days of high fevers with drenching sweats, severe frontal headache and aching muscles. He has no cough, rash, joint swelling or diarrhoea.

He has not travelled overseas and has no tick bite or freshwater exposure. He drinks little alcohol and takes no medication. Blood cultures taken on arrival are negative at 48 hours and a chest radiograph is normal. His employer runs a vaccination program for new staff but he had not yet been assessed for it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: No rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 142 U/L (less than 40); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures negative at 48 hours; chest radiograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin for presumed leptospirosis and repeat blood cultures now
options.rationale: Leptospirosis is the near alternative in this occupational group but typically follows freshwater or rodent urine exposure and causes conjunctival suffusion and renal impairment, which are absent here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give the vaccine now to protect him and start doxycycline empirically at the same time
options.rationale: Vaccinating a person with existing immunity or current infection can cause a severe local or systemic reaction, which is why skin and serological screening always precedes the vaccine (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Send acute serology with a convalescent sample planned, and start empirical doxycycline
options.rationale: Q fever is a culture negative zoonosis of abattoir workers diagnosed on paired serology, and doxycycline is started empirically because treatment within the first week of illness shortens it substantially (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate to investigate the fever with thrombocytopenia and hepatitis
options.rationale: Marrow examination is for suspected haematological malignancy or an unexplained pancytopenia, and a mild isolated thrombocytopenia with transaminitis in an acute zoonotic illness does not require it (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Q Fever).

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and advise review only if the fevers persist beyond a fortnight
options.rationale: Delaying treatment misses the window in which antibiotics shorten the illness and risks progression to hepatitis, endocarditis or a chronic fatigue syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii and is acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected cattle, sheep, goats and kangaroos, which concentrates risk in abattoir workers, farmers, shearers, veterinarians and their household contacts. It presents as an abrupt febrile illness with severe headache, myalgia and sweats, frequently with mild transaminitis and thrombocytopenia and a normal white cell count, and it does not grow on routine blood cultures, so the diagnosis rests on paired acute and convalescent serology or on polymerase chain reaction early in the illness. Doxycycline is the treatment and works best when started within the first week, which is why it is given empirically while serology is pending. Australia has a licensed Q fever vaccine, and because it can cause severe reactions in people already immune, both a skin test and serology are mandatory before administration and the vaccine cannot be given during acute infection.
key_points: Ask about abattoir, farm, shearing and veterinary exposure in any undifferentiated fever
Blood cultures are negative because the organism does not grow on routine media
Diagnosis is by paired serology or early polymerase chain reaction testing
Doxycycline is most effective when started within the first week of illness
Skin testing and serology are mandatory before Q fever vaccination
explanation.pearls: Persisting fever with a new murmur months after Q fever suggests chronic infection with endocarditis, which requires prolonged doxycycline combined with hydroxychloroquine rather than a repeat short course.

subtopic_detail: Mandatory arterial assessment before applying compression to a chronic lower limb ulcer
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 68 year old woman has had a shallow ulcer above the right medial malleolus for four months. It weeps a lot, is only mildly uncomfortable and improves when she puts her feet up in the evening.

The surrounding skin is brown stained and firm with a bottle shaped lower leg, and there is pitting oedema to mid calf. She has type 2 diabetes for twelve years and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. She has no rest pain and no night pain. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are difficult to feel through the oedema. A district nurse has asked you to authorise four layer compression bandaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 142/84, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Shallow irregular ulcer with a granulating base above the right medial malleolus, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, pitting oedema to mid calf, foot warm with capillary refill under 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 68 mmol/mol (less than 53); ulcer swab shows mixed skin flora; no vascular studies performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply four layer compression bandaging now and review the ulcer size again in two weeks
options.rationale: Compression is the correct treatment for venous ulceration but applying it over undiagnosed arterial disease can precipitate tissue necrosis and limb loss (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.text: Take a deep wound swab and start oral flucloxacillin for two weeks before dressing it
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised and mixed flora on a swab does not indicate infection, so antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis or systemic features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Measure the ankle brachial pressure index before deciding on the compression regimen
options.rationale: The index determines whether compression is safe and at what strength, and the pulses cannot be assessed clinically through this degree of oedema (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.text: Refer for punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude a malignant cause of the ulceration
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for an ulcer with rolled or everted edges or one that fails to heal after three months of appropriate treatment, and no adequate treatment has yet been given (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

options.text: Refer urgently to vascular surgery for angiography and consideration of arterial bypass
options.rationale: Urgent revascularisation is for critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, tissue loss and absent perfusion, and her foot is warm with adequate capillary refill and no rest pain (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

explanation.summary: Compression is the single most effective treatment for a venous leg ulcer and roughly doubles the healing rate, but it is dangerous if significant arterial disease coexists, so the ankle brachial pressure index is measured before any compression is applied. An index between 0.8 and 1.3 permits full strength compression, 0.5 to 0.8 allows only reduced compression with specialist input, and below 0.5 compression is contraindicated and the patient needs vascular assessment. Diabetes and chronic kidney disease cause medial arterial calcification that makes the vessels incompressible, so an index above 1.3 is falsely reassuring and should prompt a toe brachial index or arterial duplex instead. The venous phenotype of a shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus with haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and relief on elevation contrasts with the arterial phenotype of a punched out painful ulcer over pressure points or toes with a cool foot and night pain relieved by hanging the leg down.
key_points: Never apply compression before measuring the ankle brachial pressure index
An index of 0.8 to 1.3 permits full strength compression
Diabetes and renal disease can falsely elevate the index through calcified vessels
Mixed flora on a swab is colonisation and does not warrant antibiotics
Biopsy an ulcer that fails to heal after three months of adequate treatment
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 in a long standing diabetic is a warning of incompressible calcified vessels rather than good perfusion, and the toe brachial index is the test that gives a truthful answer.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

subtopic_detail: Treatment route decision for cobalamin deficiency with neurological involvement in a metformin user
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes for nine years describes six months of numbness and pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid calf, and says he has become unsteady in the dark and in the shower with his eyes shut.

He has taken metformin 2 g daily throughout and has no other regular medication and no proton pump inhibitor. He eats meat and dairy and drinks two standard drinks a week. Vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes and the Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent but both plantar responses are extensor.

data_table.Examination: Absent vibration at ankles, impaired proprioception at both great toes, positive Romberg, absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses, no pallor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100); serum vitamin B12 118 pmol/L (150-700); folate normal; glycated haemoglobin 58 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop metformin, start insulin and recheck the vitamin B12 concentration in three months
options.rationale: Stopping metformin removes the cause of ongoing malabsorption but does nothing for the existing deficit, and three months of untreated cord involvement risks permanent disability (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start high dose oral vitamin B12 replacement and review his neurological signs in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement is effective for uncomplicated deficiency, but neurological involvement is treated parenterally to guarantee repletion and to reverse the deficit fast (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a neuropathic pain agent and refer him to the diabetes education service for review
options.rationale: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the expected diagnosis in this man, but it does not cause impaired proprioception with extensor plantar responses, which indicate posterior column and corticospinal involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading, check intrinsic factor antibodies and review metformin
options.rationale: Posterior column and pyramidal signs with a low vitamin B12 indicate cord involvement requiring parenteral loading, and the cause must still be established since metformin and pernicious anaemia can coexist (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine before starting any replacement therapy
options.rationale: Cord imaging may show the characteristic posterior column signal change but is not needed to justify treatment, and waiting for it delays replacement in a time critical deficit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Metformin reduces ileal absorption of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in a dose and duration dependent way, so deficiency is common after several years of therapy and is easily attributed to diabetic neuropathy instead. The clinical clue that the neuropathy is not simply diabetic is involvement of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts, giving impaired vibration and joint position sense, a positive Romberg test, and the combination of absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses. Haematological and neurological manifestations do not track together, so a normal haemoglobin never excludes cord involvement and treatment must not wait for anaemia. Neurological disease is treated with parenteral hydroxocobalamin loading rather than oral replacement, the underlying cause is still investigated with intrinsic factor antibodies since pernicious anaemia can coexist, and recovery is best when treatment begins within the first months of symptoms.
key_points: Metformin causes dose and duration dependent malabsorption of vitamin B12
Absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars indicate combined cord and nerve involvement
Neurological disease can occur with a completely normal haemoglobin
Parenteral loading is used when there are neurological features
Check intrinsic factor antibodies because pernicious anaemia can coexist
explanation.pearls: Never give folate to a patient with an unexplained macrocytosis before the vitamin B12 result is back, since folate corrects the anaemia while allowing subacute combined degeneration of the cord to progress unchecked.

subtopic_detail: Investigation of dysphagia to solids and liquids after a failed empirical acid suppression trial
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar. A 41 year old woman has had 18 months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it happens with bread and with water equally, that she has learnt to stand up and arch her back to make it go down, and that she brings up undigested food from earlier in the day, particularly at night onto her pillow.

She has lost 6 kg. Four months of a proton pump inhibitor at double dose made no difference to the symptoms. Gastroscopy last month showed retained food in the oesophagus with a puckered but easily traversed gastro oesophageal junction and no mucosal abnormality, and oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field. She has never smoked and drinks minimally.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 20 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy with retained food, patent puckered gastro oesophageal junction, normal mucosa; oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field; haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with careful biopsy of the gastro oesophageal junction under sedation
options.rationale: A second endoscopy is warranted for suspected pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating tumour, which is suggested by a junction that resists passage of the scope rather than one traversed easily (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange 24 hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring off acid suppressing medication
options.rationale: Ambulatory pH testing quantifies acid exposure in refractory reflux, and dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of old food is a motility rather than an acid problem (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is used to look for an extrinsic or infiltrating malignancy once that is suspected, and it cannot demonstrate the sphincter physiology that this presentation turns on (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow and proceed to balloon dilatation of the sphincter if it is abnormal
options.rationale: A barium study is a useful adjunct but is less sensitive than manometry, and treating without subtype classification risks choosing the wrong intervention (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise the motility abnormality
options.rationale: Dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a normal endoscopy points to a motility disorder, and manometry is the diagnostic standard that also determines the subtype guiding treatment (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

explanation.summary: The first discriminator in dysphagia is whether it affects solids alone or solids and liquids equally, because a mechanical obstruction such as a stricture, ring or tumour causes progressive solid dysphagia while a motility disorder affects both from the outset. Achalasia arises from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with absent peristalsis, and it typically presents with years of symptoms, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough or soiling of the pillow, weight loss and a poor response to acid suppression. Endoscopy is performed first, primarily to exclude pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro oesophageal junction, but it is normal or shows only retained food, so high resolution manometry is the test that makes the diagnosis and assigns the subtype. That subtype matters directly, since type II responds well to pneumatic dilatation or myotomy, type III spastic disease favours a tailored longer myotomy, and treatment choice cannot be made without it.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids equally from the outset suggests a motility disorder
Regurgitation of undigested food and nocturnal soiling of the pillow are characteristic
Endoscopy is done first mainly to exclude a tumour mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Subtype determines whether dilatation or myotomy is the better treatment
explanation.pearls: Suspect pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating gastro oesophageal junction tumour when symptoms have lasted under six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over 55, since manometry cannot distinguish it from primary achalasia.

subtopic_detail: Treatment threshold and target in genetically confirmed iron overload with normal organ function
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 48 year old man whose brother was recently diagnosed with an inherited iron overload disorder. He feels well, and specifically denies joint pain, skin darkening or loss of libido.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements or iron tablets. Genetic testing confirms he carries two copies of the C282Y variant. His transferrin saturation is 68 per cent and his ferritin is 890 mcg/L. His liver enzymes, fasting glucose and echocardiogram are all normal, and hepatitis B and C serology are negative. He asks whether he needs treatment when he has no symptoms at all.

data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no skin pigmentation, no joint swelling, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); ferritin 890 mcg/L (30-300); alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L (less than 40); fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); haemoglobin 152 g/L (130-180); hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise a low iron diet with avoidance of red meat and recheck his ferritin in twelve months
options.rationale: Dietary iron restriction has a negligible effect on total body iron burden and cannot substitute for removing iron from the circulation (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding whether to start any treatment at all
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with raised transaminases or clinical features of liver disease, because the risk of significant fibrosis below that threshold is very low (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Start oral iron chelation therapy and monitor his ferritin and organ function every three months
options.rationale: Chelation is used when venesection is not possible, such as in transfusional overload with anaemia, and it is more toxic and far more expensive than removing blood (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Reassure him that he is asymptomatic and repeat his iron studies again in twelve months time
options.rationale: Iron accumulation is silent until organ damage is established, and treating before symptoms appear is what prevents cirrhosis, diabetes and cardiomyopathy (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Begin weekly venesection to reduce ferritin below 50 mcg/L, then move to maintenance
options.rationale: A ferritin above the reference range with a raised transferrin saturation in a C282Y homozygote indicates iron loading, and induction venesection to a low target followed by maintenance prevents end organ damage (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis; GESA: Haemochromatosis).

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in Australia is overwhelmingly due to homozygosity for the C282Y variant in the HFE gene, which is common in people of northern European ancestry, although penetrance is incomplete so many homozygotes never accumulate clinically important iron. Transferrin saturation is the earliest abnormality and ferritin reflects the accumulated burden, and treatment is indicated once ferritin exceeds the reference range even in the absence of symptoms, because the organ damage of cirrhosis, diabetes, arthropathy, hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy is largely irreversible once established. Induction venesection removes roughly 500 mL weekly, taking about 250 mg of iron each time, until ferritin falls to around 50 mcg/L, after which maintenance venesection a few times a year keeps it in the low normal range. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes identifies the group at real risk of cirrhosis who need fibrosis assessment and ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance.
key_points: C282Y homozygosity is the usual genotype and penetrance is incomplete
Raised transferrin saturation appears before ferritin rises
Treat once ferritin exceeds the reference range even without symptoms
Induction venesection targets a ferritin around 50 mcg/L before maintenance
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes prompts fibrosis assessment
explanation.pearls: First degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote should be offered genetic testing and iron studies, since identifying and venesecting an affected sibling before ferritin passes 1000 mcg/L essentially removes their cirrhosis risk.

subtopic_detail: Recognising a microangiopathy that requires plasma exchange rather than platelet transfusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward at 2 am. A 39 year old woman admitted this evening with confusion and bruising has become more agitated and is now intermittently disoriented to place. She has no fever source, no diarrhoea and takes no regular medication.

Her platelet count is 12 x10^9/L and her haemoglobin has fallen from 118 to 78 g/L over 24 hours. The blood film shows numerous red cell fragments and marked thrombocytopenia. Her international normalised ratio is 1.1, activated partial thromboplastin time is 32 seconds and fibrinogen is 3.6 g/L. Her creatinine is 118 micromol/L. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The intern has already ordered a platelet transfusion for the bruising and low count.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and bruising, fluctuating disorientation, no focal neurology, no organomegaly, no rash of purpura fulminans
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165); red cell fragments on film; international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2); fibrinogen 3.6 g/L (2.0-4.0); lactate dehydrogenase 1180 U/L (120-250); bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90); direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Proceed with the platelet transfusion and reassess her conscious state after it has run
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in this microangiopathy fuels further platelet consumption in the microcirculation and is associated with worsening ischaemic events (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Start intravenous immunoglobulin and high dose corticosteroid for immune thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia gives isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal haemoglobin and no fragments, and neither anaemia with fragmentation nor a raised lactate dehydrogenase belongs to it (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Cancel the platelets, request urgent plasma exchange and send a sample for ADAMTS13 activity
options.rationale: Fragmentation haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological change and normal coagulation identifies a thrombotic microangiopathy in which plasma exchange is life saving and must not wait for the enzyme assay (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to correct the consumptive coagulopathy present
options.rationale: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the near differential but it prolongs the clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, and both are normal here (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain before any haematological intervention
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate for focal deficits or suspected intracranial haemorrhage, and a fluctuating global conscious state without focal signs should not delay exchange (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity, usually from an acquired autoantibody, which leaves ultra large von Willebrand factor multimers in the circulation to trap platelets and shear red cells in the microvasculature. The clinical result is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragments on the film, profound thrombocytopenia, and organ ischaemia that most often manifests as fluctuating neurological signs, with fever and renal impairment variably present. The finding that separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation is a normal international normalised ratio, activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen, since this is a platelet consumptive process rather than a coagulation factor consumptive one. Untreated mortality approaches 90 per cent and falls to around 10 per cent with plasma exchange, so exchange is arranged on clinical suspicion while the ADAMTS13 sample is still in the laboratory, and platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life threatening bleeding.
key_points: Fragments with severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation define the syndrome
Normal fibrinogen and clotting times exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation
Plasma exchange is started on suspicion and not delayed for the ADAMTS13 result
Platelet transfusion can worsen microvascular thrombosis and is generally avoided
Corticosteroid and rituximab are used alongside exchange in acquired disease
explanation.pearls: Send the ADAMTS13 sample before the first plasma exchange, because exchange replaces the enzyme and a post exchange sample can produce a falsely normal activity level that obscures the diagnosis retrospectively.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic selection for severe community acquired sepsis in tropical northern Australia
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in Darwin in February. A 54 year old man with type 2 diabetes and a glycated haemoglobin of 91 mmol/mol presents with four days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain, and has become confused in the last six hours. He is a heavy drinker and works clearing drains, and there has been heavy rain for a fortnight.

He has not travelled outside the Northern Territory. His chest radiograph shows bilateral upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity on the right. Blood cultures and sputum have been sent. He has had no recent hospital admission and takes no immunosuppressive medication. He is being prepared for the intensive care unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88 per cent on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Confused and peripherally shut down, bronchial breathing in both upper zones, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no skin abscess
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 186 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0); glycated haemoglobin 91 mmol/mol (less than 53); chest radiograph with bilateral upper lobe consolidation and right sided cavitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and admission to the intensive care unit
options.rationale: That regimen covers typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia but neither agent is reliably active against the tropical pathogen that this exposure history and cavitating pattern indicate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin and a single dose of intravenous gentamicin
options.rationale: Third generation cephalosporin cover is the standard severe pneumonia regimen in temperate Australia but is inadequate for this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and to aminoglycosides (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with piperacillin tazobactam and oral oseltamivir for influenza cover
options.rationale: This targets resistant staphylococcal and hospital acquired organisms plus influenza, but he has no healthcare exposure and piperacillin tazobactam is not the recommended agent for this pathogen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous meropenem with azithromycin and rifampicin added for atypical organism cover
options.rationale: A carbapenem does cover this organism, but meropenem is reserved for neurological or very severe disease and rifampicin has no established role in the intensive phase (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftazidime with azithromycin added to cover atypical community pathogens
options.rationale: Wet season presentation in the tropical north with diabetes, alcohol use, soil and water exposure and cavitating upper lobe pneumonia indicates melioidosis, for which ceftazidime is the recommended intensive phase agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Royal Darwin Hospital Melioidosis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental organism of soil and surface water in northern Australia and South East Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the wet season when heavy rain aerosolises and mobilises the bacterium. The dominant risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney and lung disease, and it presents most often as severe pneumonia with a striking tendency to upper lobe consolidation and cavitation, frequently with bacteraemia and metastatic abscesses in the prostate, liver, spleen or bone. Its critical property for the emergency clinician is intrinsic resistance to the agents used in standard severe pneumonia regimens, including ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin, so an unrecognised case receives ineffective therapy during the hours when mortality is decided. Treatment is an intensive phase of at least two weeks of intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem, with meropenem preferred for neurological or critically severe disease, followed by three to six months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole.
key_points: Wet season presentation in tropical northern Australia is the key epidemiological clue
Diabetes and hazardous alcohol use are the dominant host risk factors
Upper lobe cavitating pneumonia with septic shock is the typical severe presentation
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin
Intensive intravenous therapy is followed by months of oral eradication treatment
explanation.pearls: Omitting the three to six month oral eradication phase after successful intravenous treatment leads to relapse in a substantial minority, which is why trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is continued long after the patient feels entirely well.

subtopic_detail: Progressive breathlessness on long term antiarrhythmic therapy with an ambiguous cardiac history
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a general clinic. A 72 year old man with persistent atrial fibrillation has had four months of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for three years for rhythm control.

He has lost 4 kg and has been febrile at home twice. He has no orthopnoea and no paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, his jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there is no peripheral oedema. Fine inspiratory crackles are audible at both bases and do not clear with coughing. His echocardiogram last week showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with normal filling pressures. A chest radiograph shows bilateral reticular shadowing that was not present two years ago, and his N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide is 96 ng/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 91 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine bibasal inspiratory crackles unchanged by coughing, no elevated jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide 96 ng/L (less than 125); thyroid stimulating hormone 3.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); chest radiograph with new bilateral reticular shadowing; transfer factor 48 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase his diuretic dose and review his weight and breathlessness again in two weeks
options.rationale: Decompensated heart failure is the expected explanation in this patient, but preserved systolic function, a normal natriuretic peptide and no congestive signs argue firmly against it (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a course of oral antibiotics for a chest infection and repeat the chest radiograph after it
options.rationale: Infection is plausible given the intermittent fevers, but four months of progressive dyspnoea with a reduced transfer factor and new reticular change is not an infective time course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Measure thyroid function and liver enzymes and continue his current dose while monitoring
options.rationale: Thyroid and hepatic monitoring is part of routine surveillance on this drug and his thyroid function is already normal, so continuing the drug allows the pulmonary process to progress (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for right heart catheterisation to assess for pulmonary hypertension as the cause
options.rationale: Invasive haemodynamic testing is for suspected pulmonary vascular disease, and diffuse reticular change with a reduced transfer factor points to the lung parenchyma instead (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Cease the amiodarone in discussion with cardiology and arrange high resolution chest tomography
options.rationale: Progressive dyspnoea with a new reticular pattern and a reduced transfer factor on long term amiodarone indicates pulmonary toxicity, and stopping the drug alongside definitive imaging is the step that changes the outcome (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life of many weeks and accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, skin, cornea and nerve, producing a distinctive spread of adverse effects that includes both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity with slate grey pigmentation, corneal microdeposits and peripheral neuropathy. Pulmonary toxicity is the most feared, affecting a few per cent of patients on long term therapy, and it usually appears as subacute interstitial pneumonitis with progressive breathlessness, dry cough, weight loss and sometimes low grade fever over weeks to months. The diagnosis is one of exclusion supported by a new interstitial pattern on imaging, a fall in transfer factor from baseline, and the absence of heart failure or infection, which is why a normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function is such a useful discriminator in a patient who also has cardiac disease. Management is prompt cessation of the drug in consultation with cardiology, corticosteroid for moderate or severe disease, and awareness that improvement is slow because the drug persists in tissue for months after the last dose.
key_points: Amiodarone accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, cornea, skin and nerve
Pulmonary toxicity presents subacutely over weeks to months, not acutely
A normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function argues against heart failure
A fall in transfer factor from baseline is the most useful physiological marker
Recovery is slow because the drug has a tissue half life of many weeks
explanation.pearls: Obtain baseline lung function including transfer factor before starting long term amiodarone, since a fall from that baseline is the earliest objective sign of pulmonary toxicity and is far more useful than a single later measurement.

subtopic_detail: Vomiting of retained food in long standing diabetes and the investigation that must precede prokinetics
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 44 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 26 years describes six months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea most afternoons and vomiting of food she recognises from the previous evening. Her weight is down 5 kg.

Her glucose readings have become erratic with unexplained hypoglycaemia one to two hours after meals followed by later hyperglycaemia. She has background retinopathy and albuminuria and takes no opioid, anticholinergic or glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her abdomen is soft with a succussion splash four hours after a meal and no palpable mass, and there is no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Her thyroid function and electrolytes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 with reduced beat to beat variation, blood pressure 128/76 lying and 106/64 standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Succussion splash four hours postprandially, soft abdomen with no mass or organomegaly, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration sense to both ankles
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 74 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits; haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start regular metoclopramide and review her symptoms and glucose readings in four weeks
options.rationale: A prokinetic is a mainstay of treatment but starting it before mechanical obstruction is excluded risks treating a stricture or tumour as a motility problem (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Refer for insertion of a percutaneous jejunostomy tube for enteral feeding and hydration
options.rationale: Post pyloric feeding is reserved for refractory disease with recurrent admissions or an inability to maintain nutrition, and she has not yet had any specific treatment (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Increase her basal insulin dose and refer her to the diabetes educator for review of technique
options.rationale: The erratic profile reflects a mismatch between insulin action and unpredictable gastric emptying, so raising basal insulin without addressing the emptying will worsen the early hypoglycaemia (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging can identify an extrinsic cause but is less sensitive than endoscopy for mucosal and pyloric lesions and does not allow biopsy (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Arrange gastroscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction, then a gastric emptying study
options.rationale: Retained food and a succussion splash require exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy before delayed emptying can be confirmed scintigraphically and treated as a motility disorder (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis is a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy and typically appears after many years of diabetes in people who already have retinopathy, nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy, so its presence in isolation should raise doubt about the diagnosis. The characteristic story is early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food eaten many hours earlier, and a particularly useful clue is glycaemic instability with hypoglycaemia soon after a meal because the insulin acts before the food is absorbed. Diagnosis requires three elements in order, namely compatible symptoms, exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy, and objective demonstration of delayed emptying by scintigraphy over four hours, and skipping the endoscopy risks missing a pyloric or antral malignancy or stricture. Treatment combines glycaemic optimisation, small low fat low fibre meals, and a prokinetic, with metoclopramide limited by tardive dyskinesia risk and domperidone requiring attention to the QT interval.
key_points: Gastroparesis usually accompanies other established microvascular complications
Postprandial hypoglycaemia followed by later hyperglycaemia is a characteristic pattern
Endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction precedes any emptying study
Scintigraphic emptying is measured over four hours rather than two
Review opioids, anticholinergics and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists as contributors
explanation.pearls: Australian and international advice restricts continuous metoclopramide to about five days because of tardive dyskinesia risk, so longer term prokinetic treatment usually means domperidone with an electrocardiogram to check the QT interval first.
